blocks.text: Course Description

This is the first part of two introductory courses for essential concepts of chemistry. Theories, laws, and definitions explained in this course will be helpful to explore more specific branches of chemistry, for instance, inorganic, organic, physical, analytical, or biochemistry. Previous experience in basic algebra will be helpful to solve problems and deduce logical conclusions using multiple theories or laws. This course will mainly focus on different parameters to understand and predict the physical and chemical properties of different compounds.
Goals
Introducing the structural features of molecules and atoms.
Students will be introduced to some important chemical reactions with real-world significance.
Explaining the significance of different thermodynamic parameters.
This course will introduce different chemical bonds and their relationship with the physical and chemical properties of substances.
Objectives
Students will understand the structure of different molecules.
Students will be able to predict the stability of different molecules towards physical and chemical change.
Students will be able to distinguish between different reactions taking place in the real world.
Students will be able to determine the impact of a chemical reaction on the environment.
Students will understand the different steps of a laboratory experiment.
Students will be able to interpret and analyze scientific data.

General Chemistry, 11th Edition
Authors: Darrell Ebbing and Steven D. Gammon

Homework assignment (100 points, 10% of the total)

Assignment will contain practice problems to help students revisit the important concepts of the preceding chapters.
Every third Friday at 5:00 pm one assignment will be posted on canvas.
Students need to submit their work in canvas by the following Monday no later than 5:00 pm.
Exams (440 points, 44% of the total)
There will be five exams throughout the semester.
85 points for the first four exams and 100 points for the final exam.
Exam will contain multiple choice questions, short and broad questions.
Except for the multiple-choice questions, students’ responses will be graded partially if the final answer is not as expected.
The first four exam will be one hour long, and the final exam will be one and half hour long.
Students should leave their smart watch and smart phone in their backpack which can be stored at the front of the class.
With proper medical proof students can take the exam online, however, the entire time they should leave their camera turned on.
The materials for the final exam will be covered from the entire course.

To encourage students to continue their improvement and learning, if a student’s final grade is higher than the average of the other four exams, then the lowest grade among the other four will be replaced with the average between the final grade and the original grade of that exam.

Academic Integrity

Academic integrity is honest, truthful and responsible conduct in all academic endeavors. The mission of Saint Louis University is "the pursuit of truth for the greater glory of God and for the service of humanity." Accordingly, all acts of falsehood demean and compromise the corporate endeavors of teaching, research, health care, and community service through which SLU embodies its mission. The University strives to prepare students for lives of personal and professional integrity and therefore regards all breaches of academic integrity as matters of serious concern.
The governing University-level Academic Integrity Policy was adopted in Spring 2015, and can be accessed on the Provost's Office website (http://www.slu.edu/provost/policies.php).

Additionally, each SLU college, school and center has adopted its own academic integrity policies, available on their respective websites. All SLU students are expected to know and abide by these policies, which detail definitions of violations, processes for reporting violations, sanctions, and appeals. Please direct questions about any facet of academic integrity to your faculty, the chair of the department of your academic program, or the dean/director of the college, school or center in which your program is housed.
Specific College of Arts and Sciences Academic Honesty Policies and Procedures may be found here (http://www.slu.edu/arts-and-sciences/student-resources/academic-honesty.php).
Title IX

Saint Louis University and its faculty are committed to supporting our students and seeking an environment that is free of bias, discrimination, and harassment. If you have encountered any form of sexual misconduct (e.g. sexual assault, sexual harassment, stalking, domestic or dating violence), we encourage you to report this to the University. If you speak with a faculty member about an incident of misconduct, that faculty member must notify SLU’s Title IX coordinator, Anna R. Kratky (DuBourg Hall, room 36; anna.kratky@slu.edu; 314-977-3886) and share the basic facts of your experience with her. The Title IX coordinator will then be available to assist you in understanding all of your options and in connecting you with all possible resources on and off campus.

If you wish to speak with a confidential source, you may contact the counselors at the University Counseling Center at 314-977-TALK. To view SLU’s sexual misconduct policy and for resources, please visit the following web addresses: http://www.slu.edu/about/safety/pdfs/sexual-misconduct-policy-version7.0.pdf.
Student Success Center

In recognition that people learn in a variety of ways and that learning is influenced by multiple factors (e.g., prior experience, study skills, learning disability), resources to support student success are available on campus. The Student Success Center assists students with academic and career related services, is located in the Busch Student Center (Suite, 331) and the School of Nursing (Suite, 114). Students who think they might benefit from these resources can find out more about:
Course-level support (e.g., faculty member, departmental resources, etc.) by asking your course instructor.

University-level support (e.g., tutoring services, university writing services, disability services, academic coaching, career services, and/or facets of curriculum planning) by visiting the Student Success Center.
Disability Services Academic Accommodations
Students with a documented disability who wish to request academic accommodations are encouraged to contact Disability Services to discuss accommodation requests and eligibility requirements.

Please contact Disability Services, located within the Student Success Center, at disability_services@slu.edu or 314.977.3484 to schedule an appointment. Confidentiality will be observed in all inquiries.

Once approved, information about the student’s eligibility for academic accommodations will be shared with course instructors via email from Disability Services and viewed within Banner via the instructor’s course roster.

blocks.text: Course Description

This course introduces the chemical principles that govern the structure, function, and interactions of biological molecules. Topics include water and biological thermodynamics; amino acids and proteins; carbohydrates, lipids, and membranes; nucleotides and nucleic acids; recombinant DNA methods; and enzyme kinetics, mechanisms, and regulation. Students will connect molecular structure to biological function, solve quantitative biochemical problems, and interpret experimental data. Prior coursework in general chemistry and organic chemistry is recommended.
Goals
Connect chemical principles to the structures and behavior of biological molecules.
Relate biomolecular structure, dynamics, and interactions to biological function.
Develop quantitative reasoning through thermodynamics, binding, and enzyme kinetics.
Use biochemical evidence to explain mechanisms and evaluate scientific conclusions.
Objectives
Students will explain how water, noncovalent interactions, and thermodynamics shape biological systems.
Students will compare amino-acid properties and relate protein sequence to three-dimensional structure and function.
Students will analyze enzyme kinetics, inhibition, catalytic mechanisms, and regulation using quantitative models.
Students will describe the structures and cellular roles of carbohydrates, lipids, membranes, nucleotides, and nucleic acids.
Students will interpret biochemical graphs, molecular structures, and experimental datasets.
Students will solve biochemical problems and communicate evidence-based conclusions clearly.

Questions may be used to revisit prior knowledge, predict an outcome, or interpret biochemical evidence.

Online quizzes (100 points, 10% of the total)

Each quiz will include conceptual, structural, and quantitative questions.

In-class activities (100 points, 10% of the total)
There will be ten individual or small-group activities worth 10 points each.
Activities may include protein-structure interpretation, pathway mapping, or enzyme-kinetics problems.
Students will receive credit for a complete, evidence-based attempt and active participation.
Selected activities will conclude with a whole-class discussion and feedback.
Reading and reflection assignments (50 points, 5% of the total)
Five reading and reflection assignments will be posted in Canvas (10 points each).
Assignments may draw on the textbook, a short research article, or a biochemical case study.
Students will identify a central claim, supporting evidence, and one remaining question.
Data-analysis quizzes (100 points, 10% of the total)
There will be five short data-analysis quizzes worth 20 points each.
Each quiz will ask students to interpret graphs, molecular structures, or experimental results.
Quizzes will follow major units and will emphasize reasoning rather than memorization.
Question formats may include calculations, multiple choice, short answers, and annotated figures.
Homework assignments (150 points, 15% of the total)
There will be five homework assignments worth 30 points each.
Assignments will combine quantitative problems, molecular interpretation, and short explanations.
Each assignment will be posted in Canvas at least one week before its due date.
Students must submit their work in Canvas by the stated deadline.
Exams (450 points, 45% of the total)
There will be four unit exams and one cumulative final exam.
Each unit exam is worth 80 points; the cumulative final exam is worth 130 points.
Exams may include multiple-choice questions, calculations, molecular structures, data interpretation, and written explanations.
Written work may receive partial credit when the reasoning is clear and scientifically supported.
Unit exams will fit within one class period; the final exam will follow the university exam schedule.
Phones, smart watches, and other unauthorized devices must be stored during exams.
Students needing testing accommodations should coordinate with Disability Services and the instructor before the exam.
The final exam will be cumulative, with emphasis on connections among biomolecular structure, energetics, and function.
If a student's final-exam percentage exceeds the lowest unit-exam percentage, the lowest unit-exam score will be replaced by the average of those two percentages.
